hints: Look at the skeletal structure and count the longest carbon chain containing the C=C double bond, then locate the Cl substituent.
walkthrough:
Number to give the double bond the lowest number**
You are sitting with $\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$. The chain is 3 carbons long with a double bond, so the parent is propene. Number from the end with the double bond, so the double bond starts at C1 and the Cl is on C3. That gives 3-chloroprop-1-ene.

hints: Think about what type of energy is needed to split $\text{Cl}_2$ into two $\text{Cl}^\bullet$ by homolytic fission.
walkthrough:
Link initiation to bond breaking**
Initiation needs $\text{Cl}-\text{Cl}$ to break homolytically to give two $\text{Cl}^\bullet$ radicals. That bond is strong and needs high energy photons. In the lab that means ultraviolet light, and in sunlight the UV component does the same job.
Final answer: UV light / sunlight

hints: In this propagation step a $\text{Cl}^\bullet$ removes an allylic H from propene to make HCl, leaving a carbon radical. Identify which reactant provides the H.
walkthrough:
Build the propagation equation**
A $\text{Cl}^\bullet$ collides with propene, $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}_3$, and abstracts an allylic hydrogen to form $\text{HCl}$. The propene loses H and becomes the propenyl radical $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}_2^\bullet$. Remember to show the dot on the Cl radical and on the carbon radical product: $$\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}_3 + \text{Cl}^\bullet \rightarrow \text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}_2^\bullet + \text{HCl}$$

hints: Recall whether free radicals can distinguish cleanly between different C-H positions or stop after one substitution.
walkthrough:
See why radicals give mixtures**
Once $\text{Cl}^\bullet$ radicals are present they attack very readily and are not selective. The product allyl chloride still has C-H bonds that can be attacked again, so dichloro and polychloro compounds form alongside allyl chloride. That mixture means a low yield of the wanted monochloro product.
Final answer: Free-radical substitution is uncontrolled so further chlorination / substitution occurs to give other chlorinated products.

hints: This is conversion of an alcohol $\text{-OH}$ to an alkyl chloride $\text{-Cl}$ without touching the C=C bond. Recall the standard reagents that replace OH by Cl.
walkthrough:
Choose a clean OH to Cl reagent**
You need to swap $\text{-OH}$ for $\text{-Cl}$ in $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}_2\text{OH}$. The classic AS reagents are phosphorus chlorides, $\text{PCl}_5$ or $\text{PCl}_3$, thionyl chloride $\text{SOCl}_2$, or concentrated $\text{HCl}$. Any one of these gives $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}_2\text{Cl}$ cleanly without free-radical side reactions.
Final answer: $\text{SOCl}_2$ or $\text{PCl}_5$ or $\text{PCl}_3$ or concentrated $\text{HCl}$

hints: Reaction 1 converts $\text{C=C}$ in allyl chloride to two $\text{-OH}$ groups while keeping the $\text{-Cl}$ intact. Think about which mild oxidant gives a diol rather than cleavage.
walkthrough:
Recognise alkene to diol**
Look at reaction 1: $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}_2\text{Cl}$ becomes $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{Cl}$. This is addition of two OH across the double bond. The specific mild condition for this is cold, dilute, acidified potassium manganate(VII). Hot concentrated $\text{KMnO}_4$ would cleave the chain, so cold and dilute is essential.
Final answer: Cold, dilute, acidified $\text{KMnO}_4$

hints: Reaction 2 converts two $\text{-OH}$ groups into two $\text{CH}_3\text{COO-}$ ester groups on heating under reflux. What is the role of concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ in ester formation?
Look at the acyl fragment $\text{CH}_3\text{COO-}$ in the product to work backwards to the carboxylic acid that supplied it.
walkthrough:
Spot esterification and the catalyst**
Reaction 2 turns a diol into a diester. Heating a carboxylic acid with an alcohol under reflux with concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is esterification, and the acid acts as a catalyst by protonating the carbonyl and speeding up the reaction.

Work back from the ester group**
Both new groups are $\text{CH}_3\text{COO-}$. An ester $\text{RCOO-R'}$ comes from acid $\text{RCOOH}$. Here $\text{R} = \text{CH}_3$, so the acid must be $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$, ethanoic acid.

Final answer: Role of concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$: catalyst
Identity of organic acid: ethanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$

hints: In reaction 3, $\text{-Cl}$ is replaced by $\text{-CN}$ using $\text{CN}^-$ from HCN / NaCN. Decide what type of attack by a nucleophile on a saturated carbon this is.
walkthrough:
Classify Cl to CN conversion**
You have $\text{R-Cl}$ going to $\text{R-CN}$. The $\text{C-Cl}$ carbon is electron poor and $\text{CN}^-$ is a nucleophile donating a pair to carbon while $\text{Cl}^-$ leaves. That is nucleophilic substitution, at AS accepted as $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ for a primary chloroalkane.
Final answer: Nucleophilic substitution

hints: Excess aqueous $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ with heating hydrolyses both functional groups in Y: what do esters and nitriles each become under acidic aqueous conditions?

Count carbons to check the $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{O}_4$ formula: the backbone from Y after hydrolysis keeps 4 carbons in a straight chain with two OH groups and one COOH group. Where must the OH groups be?
walkthrough:
Hydrolyse both esters and the nitrile**
Think of Y as $\text{CH}_3\text{COOCH}_2\text{CH(OOCCH}_3\text{)CH}_2\text{CN}$. With excess hot aqueous acid, each $\text{CH}_3\text{COO-}$ ester gives back $\text{-OH}$ plus ethanoic acid, and the $\text{-CN}$ nitrile gives $\text{-COOH}$ plus an ammonium salt.

Draw the C4 backbone**
After removing the two ethanoyl groups and converting CN to COOH, you are left with a straight 4-carbon acid: $$\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{COOH}$$ This matches $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{O}_4$ and is a 3,4-diol, 3,4-dihydroxybutanoic acid.
Final answer: Z is $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{COOH}$, 3,4-dihydroxybutanoic acid (straight 4C chain with COOH at C1 and OH groups at C3 and C4).

hints: HBr adds to $\text{C=C}$ via a carbocation intermediate. Compare the two possible carbocations that lead to the major and minor products: which is primary and which is secondary?
Recall why alkyl groups stabilise a positive carbon, consider electron donation toward the carbocation centre.
walkthrough:
Compare the two possible carbocations**
Picture $\text{H}^+$ adding first to the double bond of $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}_2\text{Cl}$. If $\text{H}^+$ adds to the terminal $\text{CH}_2$, the positive charge lands on the middle carbon giving a $2^\circ$ carbocation $\text{CH}_3\text{C}^+\text{HCH}_2\text{Cl}$. If $\text{H}^+$ adds the other way, you get a $1^\circ$ carbocation. The $2^\circ$ ion then captures $\text{Br}^-$ to give $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_2\text{Cl}$, the major product.

Explain the stability with the inductive effect**
A carbocation is stabilised when neighbouring alkyl groups push electron density toward the positive carbon. This is the positive inductive (+I) effect. The $2^\circ$ carbocation has two alkyl groups donating electrons, while the $1^\circ$ has only one, so the $2^\circ$ intermediate is lower in energy, forms faster, and leads to the major product.

Final answer: Major product forms via the more stable secondary ($2^\circ$) carbocation intermediate.
Stabilised by the positive inductive (+I) effect of alkyl groups.
